planting.note: Plant container-grown stock after the last hard frost.

directions: Tree cotoneaster grows into a large arching shrub or small multi-stemmed tree valued for its heavy late-autumn clusters of small red berries that persist into winter and draw thrushes and other fruit-eating birds. Clusters of white flowers appear in late spring against gray-green, semi-evergreen foliage. Give it an open, sunny site with room to spread, since mature specimens from the Himalayan foothills can eventually rival a small tree in size. It tolerates poor, dry soils once established and needs little supplemental water.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or early fall.

directions: Himalayan cotoneaster is an upright, semi-evergreen shrub from the Khasi Hills that holds its small dark leaves well into winter in milder climates. Small white flowers in early summer give way to abundant orange-red berries that ripen in autumn and feed overwintering birds. Because it seeds itself readily in mild, moist climates, gardeners should watch nearby open ground for volunteer seedlings and remove them promptly. It adapts to a wide range of soils and performs best with occasional pruning to maintain an open form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock after the last hard frost.

directions: Hollyberry cotoneaster is a vigorous deciduous shrub native to western China, named for its puckered, holly-textured leaves that turn red-orange in fall. Small pink-tinged white flowers in late spring are followed by large, glossy red berries borne in generous clusters, among the showiest fruit displays in the genus. The arching branches benefit from an open site with good air circulation, and once rooted the shrub tolerates drought and lean soil without complaint. In parts of the Pacific Northwest it has escaped cultivation, so gardeners there should site it away from natural woodland edges.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in early spring.

directions: Many-flowered cotoneaster is a graceful, arching deciduous shrub from central Asia that produces an unusually heavy spring display of small white flowers along its branches, denser than most cotoneasters. The flowers mature into small red berries by late summer, set against soft blue-green foliage. It is among the more cold-hardy species in the genus and withstands harsh winters and dry steppe-like conditions once its roots are established. Prune lightly after flowering only to remove dead wood, since the fountain-like branching habit is part of its appeal.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock after the last hard frost.

directions: Narrowleaf firethorn is an evergreen shrub from Yunnan province valued for persistent orange-yellow berries that often remain on the plant through much of winter, later than many coccinea-type firethorns. Small white flowers cluster along the branches in late spring, and the narrow gray-green leaves give the shrub a finer texture than more common selections. It tolerates heat, drought, and alkaline soils well, making it useful for espalier or informal barrier hedges in warmer regions. Thorny stems make it an effective security planting beneath windows.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

directions: Nepalese firethorn is a thorny evergreen shrub native to the Himalayan foothills, less often seen in cultivation than its Chinese relatives but valued by collectors for its finely toothed, glossy leaves and dense clusters of white spring flowers. Orange-red berries ripen in autumn and persist into winter, held on a densely branched, spiny framework that makes a formidable barrier hedge. It prefers a sunny, well-drained site and, once established, tolerates considerable drought. This species has contributed to several garden hybrids that combine its hardiness with the fruit display of other firethorns.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock after the last hard frost; allow room for a large mature size.

directions: Gibbs' firethorn is a robust, upright evergreen shrub from central China that produces exceptionally heavy crops of bright red berries in long-lasting clusters, among the showiest fruit displays of any firethorn species. Clusters of white flowers open in late spring on vigorous, thorny branches that can be trained against a wall or left to form a large freestanding screen. It grows considerably larger than Pyracantha coccinea cultivars and should be given generous space from the start. The species tolerates poor soils and urban pollution, and its fruit persists well into winter before birds strip it.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in a sheltered site.

directions: Chinese stranvaesia, now classified botanically as Photinia davidiana, is an evergreen shrub or small tree from western China grown for its long-lasting clusters of small red berries that often hang on through winter after surrounding leaves have reddened. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in early summer, followed by fruit that ripens by autumn. Some older leaves turn red before dropping even though the plant is substantially evergreen, giving a mixed-color effect uncommon among photinias. It prefers a sheltered site with reliable moisture and benefits from protection from harsh winter wind in colder parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in a site with part-day shade in hot climates.

directions: Beauverd's photinia is a deciduous Chinese species that grows as a large shrub or small tree, distinguished from the evergreen x fraseri hybrids by its flat clusters of white spring flowers and small fruit that ripens red before darkening toward black in autumn. Its foliage colors attractively in fall, and the open branching habit suits woodland-edge plantings rather than the clipped hedges typical of fraseri selections. It is seldom offered commercially but circulates through specialist arboretum and botanic garden seed exchanges. Give it reliably moist, well-drained soil and part shade in hotter climates to avoid leaf scorch.
